1.contenido: 1. The prolonged and terrible war declared against the divine authority of the Church has reached where it had to go: to put human society and, especially, political authority, on which public health fundamentally lies, in universal danger. A fact that we see verified especially in our time.

2.contenido: 2. These great public dangers, which are in sight, cause us serious concern as we see the safety of princes, the tranquility of States and the salvation of peoples in danger almost at all hours. And yet, the divine virtue of the Christian religion engendered the egregious foundations of the stability and order of the States from the moment it penetrated the customs and institutions of the cities. Not the smallest and last fruit of this virtue is the just and wise balance of rights and duties between princes and people. Because the precepts and examples of Christ our Lord have an admirable force to contain in their duty both those who obey and those who command and to preserve between them the union and concert of wills, which is fully in accordance with nature and from which is born the calm and undisturbed course of public affairs. For this reason, having been placed by the grace of God at the head of the Catholic Church as custodian and interpreter of the doctrine of Christ, We judge ourselves, venerable brothers, that it is the responsibility of our authority to publicly remember what Catholic truth requires of each one in this type of duties. From this exhibition will also emerge the path and the way in which public safety must be attended to in such a deplorable state of affairs.

3.contenido: 3. Although man, carried away by an arrogant spirit of rebellion, often tries to shake the restraints of authority, yet he has never been able to achieve liberation from all obedience. Necessity requires that there be some who rule in every meeting and community of men, so that society, destitute of principle or governing head, does not disappear and be deprived of achieving the end for which it was born and established. But although the total destruction of political authority in the States has not been achieved, it has nevertheless been desired to use all possible arts and means to weaken its strength and diminish its majesty. This happened mainly in the 16th century, when a pernicious novelty of opinions seduced many. From that time on, society sought not only to be given greater freedom than was fair, but also wanted to shape at its discretion the origin and constitution of the civil society of men. But there is even more. Many of our contemporaries, following in the footsteps of those who in the last century called themselves philosophers, affirm that all power comes from the people. Therefore, those who exercise power do not exercise it as their own thing, but as a mandate or delegation of the people, and in such a way that the affirmation that the same popular will that handed over power can revoke it at will has the status of law. Catholic doctrine is very different on this point, which places the origin of political power in God, as a natural and necessary principle.

4.contenido: 4. It is important to note at this point that those who are to govern the States can be chosen, in certain circumstances, by the will and judgment of the multitude, without Catholic doctrine opposing or contradicting this election. With this election the ruler is appointed, but the rights of power are not conferred. Nor is power given as a mandate, but rather the person who is to exercise it is established. This encyclical does not deal with different forms of government. There is no reason for the Church to disapprove of the government of one man or of many, as long as that government is just and serves the common good. Therefore, once justice is preserved, people are not prohibited from adopting that system of government that is most suitable and convenient to their way of being or to the institutions and customs of their elders.

5.contenido: 5. But regarding the origin of political power, the Church rightly teaches that power comes from God. This is what the Church finds clearly attested in the Holy Scriptures and in the monuments of Christian antiquity. But, furthermore, no doctrine can be thought of that is more convenient to reason or more in accordance with the good of rulers and people.

6.contenido: 6. The books of the Old Testament clearly state in many places that the true source of human authority is in God: "Through me kings reign...; Through me princes rule, and the mighty of the earth rule. And elsewhere: "Listen, you who rule over the nations..., for power was given to you by God and sovereignty by the Most High." Which is also contained in the book of Ecclesiasticus: "God gave each nation a leader." However, the men who had received these teachings from God himself gradually forgot them due to superstitious paganism, which, just as it corrupted many notions and ideas of reality, so it also adulterated the genuine idea and beauty of political authority. Later, when the light of the Christian Gospel shone, vanity gave way to truth, and again the noble and divine principle from which all authority comes became clear. Christ our Lord responded to the Roman president, who assumed the power to absolve and condemn him: "You would have no power over me if it had not been given to you from above." Text commented by Saint Augustine, who says: "Let us learn what he said, which is the same thing taught by the Apostle, namely: that there is no authority except through God." The incorrupt voice of the apostles echoed the doctrine and precepts of Jesus Christ. Exalted and full of gravity is the sentence of Saint Paul addressed to the Romans, subject to the power of the pagan emperors: There is no authority except through God. From which statement, as a cause, he deduces the following conclusion: Authority is the minister of God.

7.contenido: 7. The Fathers of the Church sought with all diligence to affirm and propagate this same doctrine, in which they had been taught. "Let us not attribute," says Saint Augustine, "except to the true God alone the power to give the kingdom and power." Saint John Chrysostom reiterates the same teaching: "That there are principalities and that some rule and others are subjects, it does not happen by chance or recklessly..., but by divine wisdom." Saint Gregory the Great testified to the same thing with these words: "We confess that power comes from heaven to emperors and kings." The same holy Doctors also sought to illustrate these same precepts even with the natural light of reason alone, so that they must appear right and true even to those who have no other guide than reason.

8.contenido: 8. Those who seek to place the origin of civil society in the free consent of men, placing in this source the principle of all political authority, affirm that each man gave up something of his own right and that he voluntarily surrendered himself to the power of him to whom the total sum of those rights had corresponded. But there is a big mistake here, which consists of not seeing the obvious. Men are not a solitary and wandering species. Men enjoy free will, but they were born to form a natural community. Furthermore, the pact they preach is clearly an invented fiction and does not serve to give political authority the strength, dignity and firmness that the defense of the republic and the common utility of the citizens require. Authority will only have this majesty and universal foundation if it is recognized that it comes from God as an august and most holy source.

9.contenido: 9. It is impossible to find a truer and more useful teaching than the one presented. Because if the political power of rulers is a participation in divine power, political power achieves for this same reason a dignity greater than merely human. Not precisely the impious and absurd dignity claimed by the pagan emperors, who sometimes demanded divine honors, but the true and solid dignity, which is received by a special gift from God. But in addition, the governed must obey the rulers as God himself, not out of fear of punishment, but out of respect for the majesty, not with a feeling of servitude, but as a duty of conscience. Therefore, authority will remain in its true place much more firmly. For, citizens experiencing the force of this duty, they will necessarily flee from evil and contumacy, since they must be persuaded that those who resist political power resist the divine will, and that those who refuse to honor rulers refuse to honor God himself.

10.contenido: 10. According to this doctrine, the apostle Saint Paul particularly instructed the Romans. He wrote to them about the reverence due to supreme rulers, with such great authority and weight that it seems no order could be given with greater severity: "You must all be subject to the superior authorities... There is no authority except by God, and those that exist have been ordained by God, so that whoever resists authority resists the disposition of God, and those who resist it attract condemnation upon themselves... It is necessary to submit not only for fear of punishment, but for conscience." And along this same line moves the noble sentence of Saint Peter, Prince of the Apostles: «For the love of the Lord, be subject to all human authority â€œconstituted among youâ€, whether to the emperor, as sovereign, or to the governors, as his delegates, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of the good. Such is the will of God."

11.contenido: 11. Men have only one reason for not obeying: when something is demanded of them that is openly repugnant to natural law or divine law. All things in which the natural law or the will of God are violated cannot be commanded or executed. If, then, it happens that man is forced to do one of two things, either to despise the commands of God, or to despise the order of princes, he must obey Jesus Christ, who commands to give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. Following the example of the apostles, we must respond cheerfully: "It is necessary to obey God before men." However, those who act in this way cannot be accused of breaking due obedience, because if the will of the rulers contradicts the will and laws of God, the rulers exceed the scope of their power and pervert justice. Not even in this case can his authority be valid, because this authority, without justice, is null.

12.contenido: 12. But in order for justice to be maintained in the exercise of power, it is extremely important that those who govern the States understand that political power has not been given for the benefit of an individual and that the government of the republic cannot be exercised for the benefit of those to whom it has been entrusted, but for the good of the subjects entrusted to them. Let princes take the example of the greatest God, from whom authority has come to them. Propose the image of God in the administration of the republic, govern the people with equity and fidelity and mix paternal charity with the necessary severity. For this reason the Sacred Letters warn the princes that they too have to one day give an account to the King of kings and Lord of lords. If they abandon their duty, they will in no way be able to avoid the severity of God. «Because, being ministers of his kingdom, you did not judge rightly... Terrible and sudden it will come upon you, because severe judgment must be imposed on those who rule; The Lord of all does not fear anyone nor will he respect the greatness of any, because He has made the small and the great and equally cares for all; "But the powerful are threatened by a powerful inquisition."

13.contenido: 13. With these precepts that ensure the republic, every opportunity and even every desire for sedition is removed. And from now on, the tranquility and security of the States are consolidated to the honor and security of the princes. The dignity of the citizens is also saved, who are granted to preserve, in their very obedience, the decorum appropriate to the excellence of man. They know very well that in the eyes of God there is neither slave nor free, that there is only one Lord of all, rich for all who call upon him, and that they are subject and obey princes, because these are in a certain way an image of God, whom to serve is to reign.

14.contenido: 14. The Church has always sought to ensure that this Christian conception of political power is not only imprinted on the minds, but also expressed in public life and in the customs of the people. While the pagan emperors sat on the throne of the State, who by superstition were incapable of attaining this conception of power which we have outlined, the Church sought to instil it in the minds of the people, who, as soon as they accepted the Christian institutions, had to adjust their lives to them. And so the Shepherds of souls, renewing the examples of the apostle Saint Paul, devoted themselves, with great care and diligence, to preaching to the people to live submissively to princes and authorities and to obey them. Likewise, that they pray to God for all men, but especially for emperors and for all those constituted in dignity, because this is good and pleasing before God our Savior. Of all of which the ancient Christians left us brilliant teachings, because being unjustly and cruelly tormented by the pagan emperors, they never stopped conducting themselves with obedience and submission, in such terms that it clearly seemed that the emperors were stubborn in cruelty and the Christians in obedience. This Christian modesty was so great and the will to obey was so certain that it could not be obscured by the malicious slanders of the enemies. Therefore, those who were to publicly defend Christianity in the presence of the emperors mainly demonstrated with this argument that it was unjust to punish Christians according to the laws, since they lived in accordance with them in the eyes of all, to set an example of observance. Thus Athenagoras spoke with complete confidence to Marcus Aurelius and his son Lucius Aurelius Commodus: "You allow us, who do no evil, but rather conduct ourselves with all piety and justice, not only with respect to God, but also with respect to the Empire, to be persecuted, despoiled, exiled." In the same way, Tertullian publicly praised the Christians, because they were, among all, the best and safest friends of the empire: "The Christian is not the enemy of anyone, not even of the emperor, whom, knowing that he is constituted by God, he must love, respect, honor and want to be saved along with the entire Roman Empire." And he did not hesitate to affirm that in the confines of the empire the number of its enemies decreased the more the number of Christians grew: "Now you have few enemies, because Christians are the majority, since in almost all the cities almost all the citizens are Christians." We also have a distinguished testimony of this same reality in the Epistle to Diognetus, which confirms that at that time Christians had become accustomed not only to serving and obeying the laws, but that they fulfilled all their duties with greater perfection than that which the laws required: "Christians obey the promulgated laws and with their way of life they go even further than what the laws command."

15.contenido: 15. However, the issue changed radically when imperial edicts and threats from the praetors ordered them to separate from the Christian faith or fail in any way to fulfill the duties that it imposed on them. They did not hesitate then to disobey men to obey and please God. However, even in these circumstances there was no one who tried to promote sedition or undermine the majesty of the emperor, nor did they ever claim anything other than to confess themselves as Christians, to truly be so, and to preserve their faith intact. They did not intend to resist in any way, but marched happy and joyful, as never before, to the bloody rack, where the magnitude of the torments was overcome by the greatness of soul of the Christians. For this reason, the effectiveness of Christian principles was also honored in the army at that time. It was an outstanding quality of the Christian soldier to combine perfect compliance with military discipline with courage against any test and to maintain unalterable loyalty to the emperor linked to his bravery. Only when acts contrary to faith or reason were demanded of them, such as the violation of divine rights or the bloody death of defenseless disciples of Christ, only then did they refuse obedience to the emperor, preferring to abandon their weapons and allow themselves to be killed by religion rather than rebel against public authority with mutinies and uprisings.

16.contenido: 16. When the States passed into the hands of Christian princes, the Church put more effort into declaring and teaching everything that is sacred in the authority of the rulers. With these teachings, it was achieved that the people, when they thought about authority, became accustomed to seeing in the rulers an image of divine majesty, which encouraged them to have greater respect and love for them. For this reason, the Church wisely ordered that the kings be consecrated with sacred rites, as was commanded by God himself in the Old Testament. When civil society, emerging from the ruins of the Roman Empire, was once again opened to the hope of Christian greatness, the Roman Pontiffs consecrated civil power in a unique way with the imperium sacrum. Civil authority thus acquired an unknown dignity. And there is no doubt that this institution would have been greatly useful, both for religious society and for civil society, if the princes and people had sought what the Church was seeking. As long as a concordant friendship reigned between both powers, public tranquility and prosperity were preserved. If ever the people incurred the sin of rebellion, the Church, a born conciliator of tranquility, immediately arrived, exhorting everyone to fulfill their duties and restraining the impulses of concupiscence, partly with persuasion and partly with her authority. In a similar way, if the kings sinned in the exercise of power, the Church appeared before them and, reminding them of the rights of the people, their needs and right aspirations, advised them of justice, clemency and kindness. For this reason, the influence of the Church has been resorted to many times to ward off the dangers of revolutions and civil wars.

17.contenido: 17. On the contrary, the theories about political authority, invented by certain modern authors, have already brought serious trouble to humanity, and it is greatly to be feared that, as time goes by, they will bring us greater evils. To deny that God is the source and origin of political authority is to strip it of all its dignity and all its vigor. As for the thesis that political power depends on the discretion of the crowd, first of all, they are wrong to think that way. And, secondly, they leave sovereignty based on a foundation that is too weak and inconsistent. Because the popular passions, stimulated by these opinions as with so many other incentives, rise with greater insolence and, to the great damage of the republic, precipitate, down an easy slope, into clandestine movements and open seditions. The consequences of the so-called Reformation prove these facts. Their leaders and collaborators undermined the foundations of civil society and ecclesiastical society with the pickaxe of new doctrines and provoked sudden riots and daring rebellions, mainly in Germany. And this with such a fever of civil war and death that almost no territory was left free from the cruelty of the mobs. From that heresy, a false philosophy was born in the last century, the so-called new law, popular sovereignty and uncontrolled license, which many consider to be the only freedom. From here we have arrived at those recent errors called communism, socialism and nihilism, a shameful plague and threat of death for civil society. And yet, there are many who strive to extend the empire of such great evils and, under the pretext of favoring the people, have caused many fires and ruins. The events that we remember here are neither unknown nor very distant.

18.contenido: 18. And the worst of all is that princes, in the midst of so many dangers, lack effective remedies to restore public discipline and pacify spirits. They arm themselves with the authority of the laws and think that they will be able to repress the rioters with severe penalties. They proceed with righteousness. But it is worth seriously warning that the effectiveness of punishment is not so great that it alone can preserve order in the States. Fear, as Saint Thomas teaches, "is a weak foundation, because those who submit out of fear, when they see the opportunity to escape unpunished, rise up against the rulers with greater fury the greater the forced subjection, imposed solely by fear. And, furthermore, exaggerated fear drags many to despair, and despair boldly launches itself into the most atrocious resolutions. Experience has sufficiently demonstrated the great truth of these statements.

19.contenido: 19. Therefore, it must be recognized that the Roman Pontiffs did a great service to the common good when they sought to break the restless and inflated pride of the innovators by warning of the danger that they constituted for civil society. Worthy of mention in this regard is the statement addressed by Clement VII to Ferdinand, king of Bohemia and Hungary: "The cause of faith also includes the dignity and usefulness, both of yourself and of other sovereigns, since it is not possible to attack the faith without serious ruin of your own interests, which has recently been proven in some of those territories." In this same line, the provident firmness of our predecessors has shone, especially Clement XII, Benedict XIV and Leo We ourselves have denounced many times the seriousness of the dangers that threaten us. And we have indicated at the same time the best remedy to ward them off. We have offered princes and all rulers the support of the Church. We have exhorted people to take advantage of the spiritual goods that the Church provides them. Now again we make to the kings the offer of this support, the firmest of all, and we vehemently admonish them in the Lord to defend religion, and in the interest of the State itself to grant to the Church that freedom of which it cannot be deprived without injustice and perdition to all. The Church of Christ cannot be suspected by princes or frowned upon by the people. The Church admonishes princes to exercise justice and not to deviate in the slightest from their duties. But at the same time and in many ways it strengthens and promotes his authority. It recognizes and declares that the affairs of the civil sphere are under the power and jurisdiction of the rulers. But in matters that affect simultaneously, although for different reasons, the civil power and the ecclesiastical power, the Church wants both to proceed by common agreement and that concord reigns between them that avoids disastrous disputes for both parties. As far as the people are concerned, the Church has been founded for the salvation of all men and has always loved them as a mother. It is the Church that, under the guidance of charity, has known how to imbue meekness in souls, humanity in customs, equity in laws, and always a friend of honest freedom, has always had the custom and practice of condemning tyranny. This custom, innate in the Church, has been expressed by Saint Augustine with as much concision as clarity in these words: "[The Church] teaches that kings take care of the people, that all people submit to their kings, showing how not everything is due to everyone, although clarity is due to everyone and injustice to no one."

20.contenido: 20. For these reasons, venerable brothers, your work will be very useful and totally healthy if you consult with Us about all the enterprises that by divine order you must carry out to remove these dangerous damages from human society. See to it that the precepts established by the Catholic Church regarding the political power of the duty of obedience are understood and diligently fulfilled by all men. As censors and teachers that you are, tirelessly admonish the people to flee from forbidden sects, to abhor conspiracies and to attempt nothing by means of revolution. Let everyone understand that, when you obey rulers for the sake of God, your obedience is a reasonable gift. But since it is God who gives victory to kings and grants people rest in the abode of peace, in the habitation of safety and in the asylum of rest, it is absolutely necessary to insistently beseech him to bend the will of all towards goodness and truth, to repress anger and restore to the entire world the peace and tranquility long desired.

21.contenido: 21. So that hope in prayer may be firmer, let us make the Virgin Mary, famous Mother of God, helper of Christians and protector of the human race, as intercessors; to Saint Joseph, her most chaste husband, in whose patronage the entire Church greatly trusts; to the apostles Saint Peter and Saint Paul, guardians and defenders of the Christian name.
